newsitem.title: USA: Choose words, tools carefully to improve Web searches.
newsitem.headline: Choose words, tools carefully to improve Web searches.

text.p: The Bible says, seek and ye shall find. But anybody who's ever done a Web search knows, it ain't that easy.
Locating information on the Web can be agonizing, even for people who know a Boolean qualifier from a relevancy ranking.

But whether old hand or net novice, you can improve your search results if you think about what you're after before starting, choose words carefully and use the right tools, top Internet search experts said.
Practice helps, too.
"The more familiar you are with the Web, the better your searches are going to be. Surf away," said Brian Pinkerton, creator of the Webcrawler (http://www.webcrawler.com) Web directory.
As the Web has grown, so have services to help people find information on it. Today there are dozens, including search engines, directories, indexes, and tools for locating maps and graphics.

But more isn't always better. Among the most frequent Web search mistakes: using words that are too common, making requests that are too general or specific, and failing to rephrase a search request if the first try didn't hit the mark, experts said.
"Avoid fixating on a particular form for your query," said Michael "Fuzzy" Mauldin, developer of the Lycos (http://www.lycos.com) search engine and the company's chief scientist.

"If it's not working throw out part of it. If you looked up 'Internet home page making' and the first hits you got back were junk, drop 'Internet' and try 'home page making.' By changing the way you phrase a query you can have dramatically different results," Mauldin said.
Rule No. 1 is to know what you're after before you start. Paradoxical as it sounds, if you do, you'll be more likely to choose the right search tool.

If you're hunting for something specific, such as all mentions of your favourite TV show, a Web search engine such as Excite, Infoseek (http://www.infoseek.com) or Digital's Alta Vista (http://altavista.digital.com) is the way to go, experts said.
Search engines use computer programmes to constantly crawl through millions of individual Web pages to build a massive index. Lycos' index is up to 70 million pages, and Excite has 50 million.

But if you're just browsing or researching a particular subject, a Web directory might be more suitable. Directories are created by human indexers who eyeball each site to find the creme de la creme, the fraction of all Web pages they deem the highest quality or most popular.

Once you've chosen your tools, turn to the search itself. Start by selecting a number of key words or a phrase that relates to the subject, keeping in mind that too few words could turn up tens of thousands of "hits" -- including a lot of duds -- but too many words could fail to turn up anything.

People often forget to use quotation marks to enclose a phrase. If they don't, a search engine will look for any appearance of the words in the document, not just when they're strung together, said Harold Stusnick, on the editorial team at Web directory Yahoo (http://www.yahoo.com), which currently lists 600,000 pages.

Another way to refine a search is to use Boolean operations, logical expressions such as "and," "or" and "not", that act to limit a search. Most search engines and directories accept Boolean logic, but since each works a bit differently it helps to acquaint yourself with the way a particular service operates, experts said.

Many search engines and Web directories return search results rated by how closely they matched the request; most often this relevancy ranking is expressed as a percentage. Excite goes one step further, offering a "More Like This" feature that lets users use the results of one search to find more information just like it.

Other search resources have their own special bells and whistles. On Lycos, putting a "$" behind a string of letters will return all words beginning with those letters. Yahoo offers an "Image Surfer" that lets people look up graphics.
Often overlooked are speciality search tools, indexes built by professionals or amateur experts in a subject.

One place to find these is search.com, (http://www.search.com), a Web site created by cyberspace publisher cnet (http://www.cnet.com) as a guide to all kinds of Web-based searching. In addition to listing links to the most popular search engines and directories, search.com lists speciality directories in 25 subjects, from automobiles to travel.
A few companies have come out with software they claim makes Web searches more effective.

One programme is Quarterdeck's WebCompass 2.0 (http://www.quarterdeck.com/qdeck/products/webcompass/), which sifts through 35 search resources at once, ranks results, saves searches and can be customised to do searches on company intranets. The software runs on Windows 95 or NT and is sold through retail stores and Quarterdeck's Web site.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
